newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Safrica's Mandela says supports Mbeki as successor.
newsitem.headline: Safrica's Mandela says supports Mbeki as successor.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said he would welcome the choice of his deputy Thabo Mbeki if he was elected successor.
But Mandela said it was not his job to choose who filled his shoes, and also played down his own role in the ruling African National Congress (ANC).

"If the organisation elected Thabo Mbeki I would fully support that. He is highly capable, smart, influential and committed," Mandela said in a joint interview with South Africa's state broadcaster and CNN.
"I have no doubt that any of the leaders of the ANC would produce results far above what the present incumbent (Mandela) has achieved," he said.

Repeating comments made earlier this year when he was perceived to be anointing Mbeki, Mandela said he would welcome the choice of his deputy, who has assumed more and more responsibility for the daily business of government.

Mandela's ANC on Monday slapped down a newspaper report that the president had disavowed Mbeki as his likely successor. The strong denial reflected South Africa's sensitivity to reports of potential political instability and the damage for its immediate economic health.
Foreign exchange dealers said the banner headline had unnerved an already fragile rand, which at one point on Monday shed nearly two cents against the U.S. dollar.

Mbeki, deputy president and heir apparent to South Africa's first black president, is on a mission to Europe to increase trade and investment -- the latest in a series of high-profile foreign trips seen as grooming for his eventual succession.

The report in Johannesburg's The Star daily said Mandela had dropped a "bombshell" at the weekend, warning ANC executive that he did not endorse Mbeki as its next leader and had also said so in a weekend newspaper interview.
In the interview, with correspondents of the New York Times, The Times and Sowetan, Mandela had stressed that it was not up to him to choose the country's next leader.
It was a "misconception" that he had tapped Mbeki for the job, since that was the prerogative of his party's executive, Mandela told the newspapers.
The Star quoted an ANC executive source as saying "everyone was shocked" by Mandela's announcement, which the source said would trigger a race for the presidency.
This was hotly denied on Monday.
The ANC said Mandela had underlined his support for his deputy. In a tough statement the ANC said: "The story in The Star is nothing but superficial sensationalism signifying nothing."

Mandela, 78, constantly tries to reassure foreign investors that his retirement will not set the country adrift. He has declared his determination to step down as president in 1999, when general elections are due.
